extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact blister skin forms a sterile barrier against infection; keep it unpopped and protect it with a moleskin doughnut pad.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a friction blister on your fingers immediately after a climb speeds up skin healing on multi-day trips.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Anyone not actively belaying must stay out of the fall zone and wear a helmet to avoid being struck by dislodged rock or dropped gear.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standing directly beneath the active climber gives the ground crew the best view to spot falling gear or loose rock.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rubbing frozen tissue causes severe cellular damage from ice crystals; rewarm frostbitten skin gently in lukewarm water around 100 degrees F.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing frostbitten fingers vigorously near a camp stove restores circulation faster after a cold weather climb.

extra_misconceptions.fact: High salt concentrations and caffeine worsen cellular dehydration; move the climber to shade and give small sips of cool water or electrolytes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving salt tablets and cold caffeinated soda to a dizzy climber rapidly reverses dehydration at a sunny crag.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to tissue integrity when a rope burn is cooled with direct ice instead of cool running water?
Which physical indicator distinguishes heat exhaustion from life-threatening heatstroke on an exposed cliff face?
Where should a Scout position themselves at the base of a cliff to remain outside the rockfall drop zone?
Why is it dangerous to apply a tourniquet or cut the skin when treating a venomous snakebite at a crag?

extra_misconceptions.fact: White chalk leaves permanent visual scars under overhangs and alters rock pH; use rock-colored chalk sparingly or clean tick marks with a brush.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Bright white gymnastics chalk is harmless to rock faces because rain washes every trace off within a single storm.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Altering natural rock permanently destroys the resource for future climbers; climb only using natural features that already exist on the wall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Chipping a small edge into blank rock improves safety without violating Leave No Trace ethics at local crags.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rope and webbing friction strips cambium bark and girdles trees; pad tree trunks with canvas protectors or use established bolted anchors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wrapping nylon webbing directly around a living cliff-edge pine tree for top-rope lowering causes no lasting harm.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Organic trash rots slowly in rocky microclimates and attracts scavengers to the crag; pack out all food scraps and human waste in WAG bags.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Burying fruit peels and biodegradable food scraps under boulders at the cliff base helps enrich poor mountain soil.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to cliffside microhabitats when climbers pry loose lichen and moss off cracks to expose handholds?
Under what condition does an active raptor nesting closure require your patrol to abandon a planned climbing route?
Which physical indicator on trees at the top of a crag shows that slings were rigged without bark protection?
Where should a climbing party stage packs and gear at the cliff base to prevent trail widening and soil erosion?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rings can catch on rock projections or carabiners during a slip and cause severe ring avulsion injuries that strip skin and tendons from bone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing a metal wedding band or class ring while climbing protects your finger bones against sharp rock cracks.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Loose clothing gets sucked into friction descenders and jams the rappel rope; wear close-fitting stretch apparel and tuck in all shirts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Baggy cargo shorts and untucked oversized hoodies are ideal for rappelling because they maximize airflow and comfort.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Denim binds tightly at the knees when high-stepping and absorbs sweat and rain, draining body heat rapidly when wind chill rises on the wall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Thick 100 percent cotton denim jeans provide the best all-weather insulation and leg flexibility on steep rock faces.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Unsecured hair easily entangles in a tube device or figure eight during a rappel; tie long hair back and tuck it inside your shirt or helmet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Letting long hair hang loose beneath a climbing helmet keeps your neck cooler without affecting belay or rappel safety.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a rappeller when loose drawstrings, long hair, or baggy shirt tails enter a loaded brake device?
Why is it dangerous to wear metal rings, watches, or dangling jewelry on your hands and wrists while climbing?
Which physical indicator during a pre-climb squat and reach test shows that your pants restrict hip mobility?
Under what condition does a heavy cotton sweatshirt become a hypothermia hazard during a windy multipitch belay?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A falling lead climber drops twice the distance above the last piece of gear plus rope stretch and belay slack, totaling well over six feet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A lead climber who falls three feet above the last protection point will drop only three feet before the rope catches.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Yosemite Decimal System ratings count upward past 5.9 to 5.10, 5.11, and beyond, with letter grades a through d subdividing 5.10 and harder.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A route rated 5.10b in the Yosemite Decimal System is easier than a 5.9 route because 10 is treated as 1.0 decimal.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Spotters never try to catch a falling climber's full weight; they protect the head and neck by guiding the torso upright onto the crash pad.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A bouldering spotter's primary job is to catch the falling climber midair so their feet never touch the ground.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A hollow drum sound when tapped indicates detached rock that can shear off under load and crush the climber or belayer below.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hollow-sounding flakes on a cliff face are stronger than solid rock because they flex slightly under hand weight.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms how far a lead climber will fall when positioned four feet above the last clipped bolt?
Which physical indicator in the Yosemite Decimal System separates a Class 4 scramble from a Class 5 technical rock climb?
Under what condition does porous sandstone become unsafe to climb even after a rainstorm has ended and skies clear?
Where should a spotter aim a boulderer's hips and torso during an unexpected fall toward the crash pad?

extra_misconceptions.fact: 'Tension' or 'Up rope' instructs the belayer to pull in loose rope, whereas 'Slack' tells the belayer to feed out extra rope to the climber.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Shouting 'Tension!' and 'Slack!' mean the exact same thing when a climber needs the belayer to tighten the rope.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The climber must wait for the belayer to confirm 'Belay on' and then reply 'Climb on' after the climber announces 'Climbing' before leaving.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A climber can step off the ground immediately after calling 'Belay on?' without waiting for the belayer's reply.

extra_misconceptions.fact: 'Off rappel' announces that the rappeller has disconnected from the rope and cleared the fall zone so the next Scout can begin rigging.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calling 'Off rappel!' tells the fireman's belayer at the bottom of the cliff to pull down smoothly on the brake rope.

extra_misconceptions.fact: 'Heads up' causes people below to look upward into the falling object; always shout 'Rock!' so everyone keeps their helmeted head down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Yelling 'Heads up!' is the standard BSA command when a rock or piece of metal hardware falls from high on a climb.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to team safety at a crowded crag when climbers omit partner names from standard verbal belay commands?
Why is it dangerous to shout the word 'Rope!' only after throwing a coiled climbing line off the top of a cliff?
Under what condition must a climber stay on the ground even after calling 'Climbing!' at the start of a route?
Which verbal command must a climber shout immediately upon dislodging a stone or dropping a carabiner from the wall?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Static rope does not elongate enough to absorb lead fall energy, generating severe impact forces that can injure the climber or rip anchors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Low-stretch static kernmantle rope is safer for lead climbing than dynamic rope because it prevents long falls.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Boot weight grinds microscopic sharp quartz and sand crystals through the sheath, where they saw through load-bearing nylon core fibers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stepping on a climbing rope at the base of a crag only makes the outer sheath dirty without harming the inner core.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bleach and high dryer heat chemically degrade nylon polymers; wash ropes only with mild rope soap in cool water and air-dry in the shade.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Washing a muddy climbing rope with bleach and drying it in a hot clothes dryer restores its original strength.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only UIAA or CE-certified kernmantle climbing ropes with a braided sheath over a continuous nylon core are approved for climbing and rappelling.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Three-strand twisted polypropylene hardware-store rope is acceptable for BSA rappelling if it feels thick enough.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to peak impact forces on a lead climber's spine if a low-stretch static rope is used instead of a dynamic line?
Which physical indicator during a hand-over-hand rope inspection reveals internal core failure beneath an intact sheath?
Why is it dangerous to retire a damaged climbing rope by tossing it whole into a camp dumpster without cutting it up?
Under what condition must a UIAA-certified dynamic rope be retired immediately even if its sheath looks brand new?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water knots can creep under cyclic loading; always dress the webbing flat without twists and leave working-end tails at least three inches long.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A water knot in tubular nylon webbing never slips once pulled tight, so trimming the tails to half an inch saves weight.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A Prusik hitch requires an accessory cord thinner than the host rope, typically 5 mm to 7 mm cord on a 10 mm to 11 mm climbing line.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A Prusik hitch grabs the main climbing rope best when tied with an accessory cord of the exact same 10 mm diameter.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Climbers tie the figure eight follow-through through both the waistbelt and leg loop tie-in points, keeping the belay loop clear.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying a figure eight follow-through directly into the harness belay loop is the standard way for a climber to tie in.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Twisted strands create uneven friction and reduce knot strength; always dress a figure eight neatly so parallel strands lie flat side by side.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Crossing and twisting the parallel strands inside a figure eight on a bight makes the knot stronger under heavy loads.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that the working-end tail on a water knot or figure eight follow-through is long enough?
Which physical indicator confirms a double fisherman's knot is tied symmetrically before tightening both halves?
What happens to the gripping friction of a Prusik hitch if the accessory cord has the same diameter as the main rope?
Where should the figure eight follow-through loop pass on a climbing harness to load both waistbelt and leg loops?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A waistbelt worn below the hip bones can slip off if a climber flips upside down; cinch it snugly above the pelvic bones so it cannot pass.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing a climbing harness loose around the lower hips is safer and more comfortable than tightening it above the pelvis.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bicycle helmets are designed for single forward road impacts, whereas UIAA climbing helmets protect the crown and sides from falling rock.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A standard bicycle helmet provides the same protection as a UIAA climbing helmet during rockfall and pendulum swings.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rope friction melts synthetic fleece instantly onto skin and lacks grip; always wear durable leather-palmed gloves when belaying or rappelling.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Synthetic fleece winter mittens are ideal for rappelling because they slide smoothly along a nylon kernmantle rope.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A tilted helmet exposes your forehead to falling rock and wall impacts; keep the rim level above your eyebrows with a snug chinstrap.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tilting a climbing helmet back onto the crown of your head gives you a clearer view of the route without reducing safety.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a seat harness waistbelt rest relative to your iliac crest hip bones to prevent inversion during a fall?
What happens to the braking hand during a fast, heavy rappel if a Scout rappels barehanded without leather gloves?
Which physical indicator on a traditional manual harness buckle confirms the webbing is properly doubled back?
Why is it dangerous to substitute a vented bicycle helmet for a UIAA-approved climbing helmet at a rock crag?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Gear loops hold only light equipment and will tear under fall loads; tie in only through the rated waist and leg tie-in points.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying the climbing rope directly into the plastic gear loops on the side of a harness is safe for top-rope climbing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Instructors and buddies perform a physical squeeze test on the gate to verify the locking sleeve is fully threaded and secure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Visual inspection alone proves a screwgate carabiner sleeve is locked before a climber leaves the ground.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The waist belt must cinch snugly above the iliac crest of the hip bones so the climber cannot slide out if flipped upside down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A harness waist belt fits properly when it rests loosely below the hip bones like a pair of casual jeans.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Webbing loosens and hardware shifts between routes, so the full five-step CHECK inspection is required before every single climb.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Once a climber passes the CHECK inspection on their first climb, subsequent climbs that morning need no re-check.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should the harness waist belt sit relative to your hip bones so you cannot slip out if inverted?
Why is it dangerous to leave rings, watches, or untucked drawcords on your body during the Clothing step?
Which physical indicator confirms a screwgate carabiner is fully locked and not cross-loaded on the gate?
What measurement of tail length beyond your figure-eight follow-through knot satisfies the Knots check?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Grabbing the live climber strand burns your hand and fails to arrest the fall; lock off by pulling the brake strand down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A belayer catches a falling climber by squeezing the live climber strand of the rope tightly above the belay device.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rockfall or a jammed hand can cause a rappeller to let go, so every BSA rappel requires an independent belay or fireman belay.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rappellers control their own descent speed, so an independent belay or bottom backup is unnecessary on short cliffs.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standing far from the wall creates excess rope stretch and pulls the belayer violently forward toward rocks during a fall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standing twenty feet back from the base of the climb gives the belayer a better view without affecting fall safety.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The backup belayer keeps a slight loop of slack three to four feet below the primary belayer so normal braking is unobstructed.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The backup belayer holds the rope tightly right next to the belay device to help pull slack through faster.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the friction inside a tabular belay device if your brake hand lifts above the device?
Where should a backup belayer stand and hold the brake strand to avoid interfering with the primary belayer?
Under what condition does a ground anchor become mandatory for the primary belayer at the base of a cliff?
Why is it dangerous to let both hands slide simultaneously along the brake strand during the PBUS cycle?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leg muscles are far stronger than arms, so efficient climbers keep straight arms for balance and push upward with their feet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Strong upper-body pull-ups are the primary way skilled rock climbers move upward on vertical faces.

extra_misconceptions.fact: 'Tension' instructs the belayer to pull in all slack and lock the brake so the climber can sit back onto the rope.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calling out 'Tension' tells the belayer to feed out extra slack so the climber can reach a higher handhold.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A direct tie-in threads a figure-eight follow-through directly through the harness waist and leg tie-in loops without hardware.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying a figure-eight on a bight and clipping it to the harness with a non-locking carabiner counts as a direct tie-in.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaning into a slab pushes your heels out and causes your feet to skate off; keep your hips directly over your soles.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pressing your chest flat against a low-angle slab increases shoe friction on smooth, featureless rock.

extra_socratic_questions: Which verbal command must you hear from your belayer before lifting your feet off the ground to start a route?
What happens to your forearm endurance if you hang from bent arms instead of pushing upward with your legs?
Why is it dangerous to pass your figure-eight follow-through knot through only the harness waist loop?
Under what condition does smearing the sole of your shoe work better than edging on a tiny rock crystal?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Jumping shock-loads the anchor system and saws the tensioned rope across sharp rock edges, risking catastrophic sheath failure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Bounding outward in long leaps down the cliff face reduces friction and cools the metal rappel device.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standing too upright pushes your feet downward off the rock; lean back at forty-five degrees with feet flat against the wall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Keeping your legs straight and your torso vertical against the cliff prevents your feet from slipping backward.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Remain on belay until you are on stable ground and signal 'Off rappel' only after the rappel rope runs free of your device.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Shouting 'Off belay' while still unthreading your rappel device saves time for the next Scout waiting at the top.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tubular rappel devices are not self-locking, so releasing the brake strand allows the rope to feed freely and drops the rappeller.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Letting go of the lower brake strand pauses a tubular rappel device automatically through internal friction.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the peak force on your top anchor if you bound and bounce down a cliff like an action movie?
Where should you position your feet and knees against the rock face to maintain stability while backing over an edge?
Which verbal signal alerts the next Scout at the top that you have disconnected your device from the rappel rope?
Why is it dangerous to grip the rappel rope tightly above the descender with your guide hand if you start slipping?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Acids and petroleum solvents break down nylon polymer chains invisibly, so any chemically contaminated rope must be retired.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Battery acid or gasoline spills on a climbing rope are harmless if the outer sheath shows no visible discoloration.

extra_misconceptions.fact: High heat melts and shrinks internal nylon core fibers, so washed ropes must air-dry flat in a shaded, ventilated area.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tumbling a muddy climbing rope in a high-heat clothes dryer restores the factory water-repellent coating.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wrapping rope around your arm introduces a half-twist per loop that creates severe kinks; use a butterfly coil or rope bag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Winding a sixty-meter climbing rope tightly around your elbow and thumb prevents tangles when flaking it out later.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Grooved aluminum edges develop sharp burrs that slice nylon sheath fibers, so deeply worn hardware must be retired immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Deep rope-wear grooves worn into an aluminum rappel device improve braking grip and extend the life of the rope.

extra_socratic_questions: Which physical indicator felt through the sheath tells you a kernmantle rope's inner core fibers are damaged?
Why is it dangerous to store nylon climbing ropes or harnesses in a garage next to car batteries or gas cans?
What happens to the tensile strength of wet nylon webbing if you dry it in direct midday sunlight or a hot dryer?
What details must be recorded in a unit rope log after a climbing session where a Scout took a hard fall?
